messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\left\lfloor \sqrt n\right\rfloor,\qquad A=m!.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid A^{\,n!}+450.
\]

Factor

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,\qquad 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

For any prime \(p\mid n\):

- If \(p\le m\), then \(p\mid m!=A\), so
  \[
  A^{n!}+450\equiv 450 \pmod p,
  \]
  forcing \(p\mid 450\).

- If \(p>m\), then \(p\nmid A\). Also \(p\mid n\) implies \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,
  \[
  A^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p,
  \]
  so
  \[
  A^{n!}+450\equiv 451 \pmod p,
  \]
  forcing \(p\mid 451\).

Thus every prime divisor of \(n\) is among

\[
2,3,5,11,41.
\]

Now suppose \(n>1230\). Then

\[
m=\left\lfloor\sqrt n\right\rfloor\ge 35,
\]

so \(11\le m\), meaning \(11\nmid n\). Hence the only possible prime divisors of \(n\) are

\[
2,3,5,41.
\]

For \(p=2,3,5\), since \(p\le m\) and \(n>1230\),

\[
v_p(A^{n!})=n!\,v_p(m!)\ge 6>v_p(450).
\]

Therefore

\[
v_p(A^{n!}+450)=v_p(450),
\]

so

\[
v_2(n)\le 1,\qquad v_3(n)\le 2,\qquad v_5(n)\le 2.
\]

Thus the part of \(n\) not divisible by \(41\) divides

\[
2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2=450.
\]

If \(41\nmid n\), then \(n\mid 450\), impossible for \(n>1230\). So \(41\mid n\).

Then \(m<41\), so \(m\le 40\). Also \(41^2\nmid n\), because \(n<(m+1)^2\le 41^2\). Hence

\[
n=41d
\]

where \(d\mid 450\). Since \(n>1230\),

\[
d>30.
\]

But \(m\le 40\) gives

\[
n\le 40^2+2\cdot 40=1680,
\]

so

\[
d=\frac n{41}<41.
\]

There is no divisor of \(450\) strictly between \(30\) and \(41\). Contradiction. Therefore no \(n>1230\) works.

It remains to check \(n=1230\). Here

\[
\left\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\right\rfloor=35,\qquad 1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

Modulo \(2,3,5\), both \(35!\) and \(450\) are divisible by those primes, so the sum is divisible by them.

Modulo \(41\), since \(35!\) is not divisible by \(41\) and \(40\mid 1230!\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Also

\[
450\equiv -1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Thus

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

So \(1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450\).

Hence the largest possible value is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
